one_liner: RocksDB fork that splits columns, re-encodes values or builds secondary indexes during compaction, for faster analytic reads than RocksDB.
what_it_does: Mycelium is a research fork of RocksDB that runs user-defined 'transformers' inside compaction. Data written as rows (JSON or Protobuf) ends up split into column groups, re-encoded as FlatBuffers, or paired with a secondary index, with no separate ETL job. Writes take the normal RocksDB Put path into a user-facing column family, and compaction moves the data into hidden destination column families. Projected reads, row reassembly and index lookups go through a wrapper (MymBroker in the probable repo, with Insert/Read/Scan/Delete/IndexRead calls), so it is a different interface and not a drop-in RocksDB replacement.
how_it_is_fast: Compaction already reads every record from its SST files and writes it back out. Mycelium does the transformation during that same pass, adding in-memory CPU work but no extra read I/O (the paper calls this 'transformation-embedded compaction'). A cross-column-family compaction writes the source family's merged L0 runs into a destination family's L0, and 'Tierveling' uses tiering for compactions that transform data and leveling for identity compactions. Reads speed up because they touch less data: a column-group split cuts the bytes read and deserialized by single-column queries, JSON-to-FlatBuffers made SSTs 34.76% smaller, and a secondary index replaces a full table scan.
when_to_use: Research or prototyping, when you want to measure whether ETL done during compaction (column-group splitting, format conversion, index building) beats a separate pipeline on your own write-heavy data.

Write-heavy ingest of wide rows (the paper uses rows of about 500 B with 32-50 columns) where later reads project one or a few columns or aggregate over key ranges. On a range MAX query, split gave 2.8x and JSON-to-FlatBuffers gave 4.25x.
Values arrive as text JSON and you can accept about 15% lower write throughput to have them stored in a compact binary format.
You need lookups on a non-key attribute and can accept an index that covers only data already compacted out of L0. The paper measured about 10% write-throughput cost for this.
when_not_to_use: Production, or anywhere you need clear licensing. The paper does not link any code. The probable repo is an anonymous single-commit snapshot with no top-level license.

Row-retrieving workloads (SELECT * point or range queries). Under the split transform, the point query (Q7) was slower than plain RocksDB at most percentiles, and the range query (Q6) had worse tail latency.

Systems bound by write throughput. Each transformation cost 10-21% of RocksDB's write throughput in the paper, and each extra cross-column-family compaction adds write amplification (the cost model's WA + n).
Delete-heavy tables with a secondary index. In the repo, every Delete scans the whole secondary-index column family to find matching entries.
Workloads that need read-your-writes through the index. Index entries are created only when data leaves L0, and IndexRead never checks the memtable or L0.

integration.form: static lib (a patched RocksDB 8.5.0 fork plus libmycelium, built with CMake, with the shared-library build forced off). In practice a source-drop from an anonymous repo.
integration.dependencies: Protobuf (protoc), FlatBuffers (flatc), jsoncpp, Apache Arrow (find_package REQUIRED, but missing from the README's list), snappy, zlib, bzip2, zstd, lz4, gflags, re2. The README also lists Boost, nlohmann-json, RapidJSON and Avro.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (-std=c++17 -Werror), CMake 3.16.3+. The paper does not state a compiler.
integration.platforms: Linux only as documented: an Ubuntu 20.04 Dockerfile and an Ubuntu 24.04 benchmark image. The CMake hardcodes /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libre2.so, so x86-64 Linux is the only tested target.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for MymBroker, although the YCSB harness drives one broker from many client threads. The paper says a transformer is locked to one compaction job at a time. TransformEpochTracker is documented as not thread-safe: there is one per SST, owned by its compaction thread.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — writes use the normal RocksDB Put path and RocksDB options. Transformed data lives in hidden internal column families that must not be written to directly. Projected reads, row reassembly and index lookups need the MymBroker wrapper, whose calls return int codes.

gotchas: In the probable repo, MymBroker::Scan ignores begin_key (it calls SeekToFirst) and ignores the column list, and the code that reassembles split rows in Read/Scan is commented out. The paper's Q2-Q7 query paths therefore cannot be reproduced from this harness as shipped.

Updates across the tree family are not atomic. The manifest edit for the source column family and the edit for each destination family are separate LogAndApply calls. Delete propagation issues a separate Delete per derived column family, and failures are logged and skipped. Crash consistency is not documented.

Secondary-index keys are field values converted to strings and joined with '%%' and '$$$KEY$$$'. Numeric fields go through std::to_string, so the index sorts lexicographically rather than numerically, and values that contain the separators are ambiguous.

Error paths print FATAL and call exit(1) instead of returning a status. More than 4 transformers, or transformer and SchemaDescriptor counts that don't match, throw std::runtime_error. The top-level CMakeLists also copies experiment/*.sh scripts that are not in the repo.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Every catalogued sibling (KVell, MatrixKV, PebblesDB, SplinterDB, Nova-LSM, NuDB, Titan) speeds up the write or key-lookup path. Mycelium is the only one that reshapes data for column-projection and non-key reads, so consider it only when those reads are the bottleneck. For anything you will ship, Titan (large values) and SplinterDB or PebblesDB (write-heavy loads) have public, licensed code.
verified_claims_summary: The test machine had two 16-core 3.0 GHz CPUs, 128 GB RAM and SATA SSDs on Ubuntu 20.04; the paper does not name the CPU model, compiler, flags or RocksDB version. After a 100 GB preload of 200M records, Mycelium's JSON-to-FlatBuffers transform cut latency 4.25x on Q2 (MAX over a key range, Zipfian keys) against RocksDB storing JSON, and split cut it 2.8x; single transforms cost 10-15% of write throughput and split+convert cost 21%. The index-query wins are measured against RocksDB full scans, and the paper's setup text is internally inconsistent (32 vs 50 columns per row, stated as about 500 B).
status_note: Research prototype only: an arXiv v1 preprint (June 2025, UC Santa Cruz) whose code is 'hidden due to anonymity'. The probable code is an anonymous review repo (one squashed commit on 2026-07-27, 0 stars, no top-level license) that has already moved to newer names (WHLSM, LSM-Grove, mRoutines), so treat it as a reference, not a dependency.
